message.abstract: <jats:p>Governments increasingly rely on digital identification systems to deliver public services, regulate economic activity, and verify citizens, yet in many developing states these systems emerge through sector-specific initiatives rather than coordinated institutional design. This article examines how fragmented identification infrastructures undermine administrative reach and state capacity, using Nigeria as a case study. Analysing the interaction between the National Identity Number, bank verification requirements, voter registration, and telecommunications SIM registration, the study shows that parallel registries produce verification inconsistencies across public institutions, limiting reliable identification of individuals. The consequences include uneven access to financial services, difficulties in welfare targeting, and higher administrative transaction costs. The central argument is that the problem is not the absence of digital identification but the lack of interoperability between systems. Fragmentation constrains the state's ability to reach populations consistently, particularly those distant from administrative centres or reliant on multiple agencies. This paper offers one of the first comprehensive multi-dimensional analyses of identification fragmentation in Nigeria, integrating development, security, and governance perspectives. It concludes that interoperability centred on the National Identity Number would simultaneously improve financial inclusion, administrative efficiency, and national security capabilities, offering a replicable model for other fragmented-system states across Africa.</jats:p>
title: Administrative Reach and State Capacity: Interoperability Failures in Nigeria's Digital Identification Infrastructure
